name: Adrenal glands
func: Two small glands sitting on top of the kidneys. Their outer layer makes cortisol and aldosterone for stress, blood sugar, salt and blood pressure; their core makes adrenaline for the fight-or-flight response.

levels.kid:
You have two **adrenal glands**, one sitting on top of each **kidney** like a little hat.

They make **adrenaline**, your body's "go fast" chemical. If a big dog barks at you, adrenaline makes your heart beat faster and gives your muscles extra energy so you can jump or run.

The adrenal glands also make a helper called **cortisol**. It keeps your energy up during busy or tough days.

And they make another helper that tells your kidneys how much **salt** and water to keep, which helps your blood pressure stay just right.
levels.hs:
The **adrenal (suprarenal) glands** are a pair of small, flattened, yellowish glands, each weighing only a few grams. They sit on the upper inner tip of each **kidney**, wrapped in fat inside **renal fascia** in the back of the abdomen (retroperitoneum). The **right adrenal** is pyramid-shaped and lies behind the **liver** and right next to the **inferior vena cava**. The **left adrenal** is crescent-shaped and lies near the **aorta**, behind the **stomach** and **pancreas**.

Each gland is really two glands in one:
- The outer **cortex** makes **steroid hormones** from cholesterol: **aldosterone**, which makes the kidneys hold on to sodium and water and raises blood pressure; and **cortisol**, the main **stress hormone**, which raises blood sugar, helps the body cope with illness and stress and calms inflammation.
- The inner **medulla** makes **adrenaline (epinephrine)** and some **noradrenaline**, which drive the **fight-or-flight** response: faster heart rate, wider airways and more blood to the muscles.

The cortex is controlled by **ACTH** from the pituitary (for cortisol) and by the **renin–angiotensin system** (for aldosterone). The medulla is switched on directly by **sympathetic nerves**.
levels.college:
The **cortex** has three zones (outside to inside), remembered as **GFR**:
- **Zona glomerulosa**: **aldosterone** (mineralocorticoid), driven mainly by **angiotensin II** and high **potassium**; it has the enzyme **aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2)**.
- **Zona fasciculata**: **cortisol** (glucocorticoid), driven by **ACTH**; the widest zone, with lipid-filled cells.
- **Zona reticularis**: a thin inner zone that makes small amounts of other weak steroids, also under ACTH control.

The **medulla** contains **chromaffin cells**, derived from the **neural crest**. They are essentially modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons: **preganglionic** fibers from the splanchnic nerves synapse on them directly and release acetylcholine. About 80% of the output is **adrenaline**. The enzyme that turns noradrenaline into adrenaline, **PNMT**, is induced by cortisol, which reaches the medulla in high concentration through blood flowing inward from the cortex.

**Blood supply** is rich, from three sources on each side: the **superior suprarenal** (from the inferior phrenic artery), **middle suprarenal** (from the aorta) and **inferior suprarenal** (from the renal artery) arteries. **Venous drainage** is by a single vein: the **right adrenal vein** is very short and enters the IVC directly, while the **left adrenal vein** drains into the **left renal vein**. The short right vein is a key surgical hazard.

Cortisol works through intracellular **glucocorticoid receptors** that act as transcription factors.
levels.phd:
Adrenal zonation is maintained by constant cell renewal: **capsular and subcapsular progenitors** (expressing **SHH** and **GLI1**, and WT1 in some states) give rise to glomerulosa cells, which then migrate inward and convert into fasciculata cells, a process traced in mouse lineage studies. **WNT/beta-catenin** signaling maintains glomerulosa identity, while **PKA** signaling from ACTH pushes cells toward a fasciculata fate; the opposing gradients shape the zonal boundary.

**Steroidogenesis** begins when **StAR** moves cholesterol into mitochondria, where **CYP11A1** makes pregnenolone; this transfer is the acute rate-limiting step stimulated by ACTH. Zone-specific enzymes then determine the product: **CYP11B1** (11-beta-hydroxylase) for cortisol in the fasciculata, and **CYP11B2** for aldosterone in the glomerulosa.

Primary aldosteronism is now understood partly at the molecular level. **Aldosterone-producing adenomas** frequently carry somatic mutations in **KCNJ5** (a potassium channel that loses selectivity, depolarizing the cell), **CACNA1D**, **ATP1A1** or **ATP2B3**, all causing excess calcium entry and autonomous aldosterone production. Normal adrenals also contain **aldosterone-producing cell clusters** carrying similar mutations.

**Cortisol** acts through **glucocorticoid** and **mineralocorticoid receptors**. Cortisol binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with high affinity, but kidney cells protect it with **11-beta-HSD2**, which inactivates cortisol to cortisone. Blocking this enzyme (as with glycyrrhizin in real licorice) causes apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

In the medulla, **chromaffin granules** store catecholamines with **chromogranin A** and ATP; exocytosis is triggered by acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors. Chromaffin cells are a classic model for studying vesicle release.
levels.expert:
Key adrenal disorders:
- **Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)**, most often autoimmune: fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, **hyperpigmentation** (from high ACTH/POMC), low sodium and high potassium. **Adrenal crisis** (shock, vomiting, collapse) is an emergency treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids. **Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome** is adrenal hemorrhage in meningococcal sepsis.
- **Cushing syndrome** (too much cortisol): central obesity, round face, purple striae, thin skin, muscle weakness, diabetes and high blood pressure. Causes: steroid medicines (most common), a pituitary adenoma (**Cushing disease**), an adrenal adenoma or ectopic ACTH. Screen with a **dexamethasone suppression test**, late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urine cortisol.
- **Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome)**: high blood pressure, often with low potassium (below about 3.5 mmol/L). Screen with the **aldosterone-to-renin ratio**; **adrenal vein sampling** decides whether one side is responsible and can be removed.
- **Pheochromocytoma**: a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the medulla causing episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with severe hypertension. Diagnosed with plasma or urine **metanephrines**; associated with **MEN2**, **VHL**, **NF1** and **SDH** mutations. Patients need alpha blockade before surgery to prevent a dangerous blood pressure surge.

**Adrenal incidentalomas** are found on about 4–7% of abdominal CTs; low attenuation on unenhanced CT (under 10 Hounsfield units) suggests a benign lipid-rich adenoma. **Adrenocortical carcinoma** is rare but aggressive.

Most adrenalectomies are done **laparoscopically** or **retroperitoneoscopically**. On the right, the surgeon controls the short adrenal vein entering the IVC early.

keyPoints: Sit on top of each kidney in the retroperitoneum; right near the IVC and liver, left near the aorta
Cortex zones (GFR): glomerulosa → aldosterone, fasciculata → cortisol, reticularis
Medulla chromaffin cells (neural crest) make adrenaline under sympathetic control
Right adrenal vein → IVC; left adrenal vein → left renal vein
Addison, Cushing, Conn syndrome and pheochromocytoma

test.explain: The outermost zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone, driven by angiotensin II and potassium.

test.q: The left adrenal vein usually drains into the:
test.explain: The right drains straight into the IVC; the left into the left renal vein.

test.q: Adrenal medulla cells that make adrenaline are called ______ cells.
test.explain: Chromaffin cells come from the neural crest and act like modified sympathetic neurons.

test.q: Episodes of headache, sweating, palpitations and very high blood pressure suggest:
test.explain: Pheochromocytoma releases catecholamines in bursts; test plasma or urine metanephrines.

test.q: The main stress hormone made by the zona fasciculata is ______.
test.explain: Cortisol raises blood sugar, supports blood pressure and suppresses inflammation.
